1. Online assessment [209 students appeared for the test]

The test was conducted on 31/7/2024 on the Hackerrank platform in college offline. There were 30 MCQs:
15 Technical - Java, SQL, DBMS, and 15 Aptitude. There was also one coding question. My question was
given a string s consisting of characters a, b, and c. In one operation, you can add any one character at any
position. The task is to convert the string into the format abcabc… We have to return the minimum number
of operations to perform this task.
Test Case:
Input: string = bb
Output: 4
Explanation:
abb -> abcb -> abcab -> abcabc (Total 4 insertions)
I solved the coding question completely and most of the mcq's and got shortlisted for the next round

Tips:

Generally, I recommend starting with the coding question. If you solve the coding question, you will likely
get shortlisted. Even if you don't find the optimal approach, try to solve it using brute force and aim to pass as
many test cases as possible. Some students did not pass all the test cases but were still shortlisted based on
MCQs and aptitude. The MCQs and aptitude questions were relatively easier, so having a basic understanding
of the fundamentals will help you.

2. [Technical Interview] [36 students appeared for this round]

a. The interview lasted for 40-45 minutes. My panel consisted of 2 members.
b. It started with "Tell me about yourself."
c. They then asked about my projects. One of my projects was based on SQL, so they told me to draw the
schema and write all the mapping relation tables. They also gave me 2 -3 SQL queries. I was not able to
solve one query, but I answered the remaining ones, which satisfied the interviewer.
d. They asked me to explain all my projects listed on my resume.
e. They asked a few basic DSA questions:

• What is an array?

• In which cases is a linked list better than an array?

• What is a stack?

• What is a queue?

f. They asked what a singleton class is, but I was not aware of it. I told them so. Later, they asked if
multiple inheritance is allowed in Java, why it is not allowed, and how to implement multiple inheritance
in Java.
g. Later he asked me "Which sport do you play ?" I answered as cricket so he asked "tell a game which
you play on board" so I mentioned chess . So he told me to implement chess game using OOP'S in java
h. We had a discussion about my ML project mentioned in my resume. Questions were like:

• Why Random Forest?

• Explain the full process of how to implement the model.

• And some basic ML questions

i.  He asked me where I see myself in 5 years.
j. Also atlast they asked if I had any questions for them (Always ask some question)

Tips:

• Know your resume very well. If you are unable to answer a question, accept that you don't know. Even

I was not able to answer some questions.

• The technical interview can be DSA-based or project-based, depending on the panelists, so be prepared

for both situations.

• If you have mentioned any projects, make sure you know everything about what you have done in that

project. Ask yourself what questions can be asked and be prepared for them.

• Search for top interview questions for Java/full stack/ML on InterviewBit/GFG and go through the

most frequently asked questions depending on your tech stack.

• Be ready for some HR questions as well; they can be asked.

3.[HR round] [Around 20 students appeared for this round]
The HR round was a bit relaxed and lasted for just 5-7 minutes.

1. It started with the question, "Tell me about yourself?"

2. Then, they asked about my family background. I mentioned that my father is a police officer.

3. She asked why I am not aiming for a government job, and we had a discussion about the private sector

versus the government sector.

4. Next, she asked what I do other than coding. I replied that I play cricket and also mentioned other

extracurricular activities I participated in during college.

5. Lastly, she asked if I had any questions for her. (Always ask some questions during this part.)

At the end, 12 students got the offer.

1. Online Assessment (209 students)

This was an online assessment(from college). Consisted of 15 MCQ Aptitude Questions + 15 MCQ
Technical Questions + 1 Coding Question on Hackerrank. Test duration was 85 mins.

• Aptitude Questions

The aptitude questions were easy to moderate. Questions were based on probability, sets, finding
missing element in series, mirror/water Images, and answering the question on the basis of a
given graph.

• Technical Questions

Questions were mostly asked on DBMS, SQL queries, JAVA basic concepts, code snippets. And
were Conceptual.

• Coding Question

server.
For Example, serverLoad = [7, 2, 7, 3], serverCapacity = [4, 1, 5, 6], The total cost of server is
calculated as - 7 * 4 + 2 * 1 + 7 * 5 + 3 * 6 = 83 (dot product of 2 initial arrays)
the position of elements in serverCapacity only. The objective is to find the sequence of
serverCapacity that results in the minimum total cost. In case multiple sequences result in the
same minimum total cost, return the sequence that is lexicographically smallest.
--- PAGE 2 ---
Java approach which i used - It was based on Greedy Algorithm. You just have to sort the
serverLoad array in descending order while keeping track of their original indexes by creating a
Pair class to store the server load and its index, then use a comparator to sort these pairs based on
the load and if loads are same then on the basis of index. Next, sort the serverCapacity array in
ascending order. Finally, create a new array to map the sorted capacities to the corresponding
loads: for each pair in the sorted serverLoad array, store the corresponding capacity from the
serverCapacity array at the original index of the pair.

2. Technical Round (36 students)

There were two interviewers in a panel and my interview lasted around 45 mins
The conversation began with a brief introduction where I shared a bit about myself and about my projects.
Following the introduction, the interviewers delved into an in-depth discussion of my projects, asking
detailed questions about the specific technologies and libraries I chose. They were particularly interested
in understanding the reason behind my choices, prompting me to explain why I opted for certain
technologies and how that benefited my projects.
The discussion then turned to the APIs I used, including how I integrated them into my projects and the
challenges I encountered. They also asked about the schemas of my project's databases, where I had to
justify my preference for MongoDB over MySQL. This led to a broader discussion about the differences
between SQL and No-SQL databases, including their respective advantages, disadvantages, and suitable
use cases.
Next, the interviewers inquired about how I implemented authentication and authorization in my projects.
I explained the strategies and technologies I used to ensure secure access control. The conversation then
shifted to front-end development, specifically React. They asked about the fundamental concepts of states
and props, their differences, and the use of hooks. This was followed by a discussion on Redux and its
role in state management within React applications.
They also explored my understanding of Java, questioning whether it is solely an object-oriented
language. To test my knowledge of data structures, they asked me to explain the internal workings of
HashMap, its differences from ArrayList, and scenarios where each would be appropriately used. Also
asked various sorting algorithms and their efficiencies.
Additionally, they presented a puzzle on the water jug problem, which required logical thinking and
problem-solving skills. Towards the end, the interviewers were keen to understand my committee
experience and how I functioned within a team. To test my abilities to manage the dynamics of teams and
my interpersonal skills, they asked me a number of scenario questions.
Overall, the interview was relaxed, providing a comfortable atmosphere for me to articulate my
experiences and knowledge. The interviewers' approach made it easy to engage in meaningful discussions
and showcase my expertise across various topics.
--- PAGE 3 ---

3. HR Round (17 students)

The HR round was relaxed and short ( around 15 mins). The interviewer began by asking about my place
of residence and my family background. Then about my future plans, including whether I had any
intentions of pursuing a master's degree. Asked me about my minor in management from SPJIMR and
wanted to know more about the specifics of that program, inquired about my experiences at SPIT
College. She asked whether I had any questions for her and asked a few.
Finally 12 students were selected!

1. I would suggest you all to maintain 8.5+ cgpa for the safer side.

2. Also I would highly recommend you all to not lie in your resumes and you must know everything

you have mentioned in your resumes. Try giving your resume to chatgpt or gemini ai and ask to
generate questions based on it

3. Oops is a must to do. Also most companies prefer java so it would be great if u do oops in java. If

your preferred language is not java (like my preferred language was python) then try to do oops in
your preferred language as well as in java because they tend to ask and also expect u to know oops in
your preferred language.

4. DSA is a must to clear OAs and interviews as well (they might ask you to code in interviews).

Leetcode is best to practice dsa. U can follow strivers sheet but i didn't do that.

5. A tip for interviews- if u are not able to answer any question asked by the interviewer but u know

some related concept around the question then u must try to tell them that like u may say that "i don't
know about this but i can tell u about this" or take guesses so that they get to know that u r not totally
blank about the topic.

6. Avoid getting basic questions wrong in the interview. They don't expect you to know or answer every

question but you must not get the basic questions wrong or they might directly reject you.

7. Don't give robotic answers like as if tum rat k ya learn kar k aaye ho. Try to be natural

8. In the end i would say that placements are 60-70% based on luck. It may happen that even after

solving all questions in oa, u might not get selected. Just don't give up. Some companies do weird ass
shortlisting which may be beyond our imagination but just don't give up. I got into Barclays after
applying in almost 12-15 companies. Sometimes u may have breakdowns and u might feel dejected
but try to not think about it because most of the things are not in our hands and we can't do anything.

He was a pure cybersecurity guy. He started by introducing himself only. Then he asked me about my area
of interest in cybersecurity and based on it he was asking questions. I was not asked anything apart from
cybersecurity in this round. It was pure cybersecurity questions only for me however others were asked
some hr questions also. At the start of the interview he was focusing on the theory part only. After that he
moved onto my resume and asked me what security measures would i have to take in my projects to prevent
cyber attacks to which i gave answers such as providing authentication authorisation etc. He was also asking
me questions on different types of cyber securities like network security, application security. Then he
moved on to situational questions like for ex i have to make any application then which application security
measures will u take care of. Then he asked me about the principles of cybersecurity (that is CIA) and asked
me how I would take care of this CIA in one of my projects mentioned in the resume. Then he asked me
about the types of attacks I knew.
I was not able to answer all of the answers nor was he expecting me to know everything. But try to think and
give answers rather than giving up on the question(who knows he/she might like ur answers).
Do CCN thoroughly as well as cybersecurity topics and your resume.
To be honest I prepared basic cybersecurity topics but he deep dived into the topics which I was not able to
answer but I tried to relate it with the topics i knew which made it easier for me and also he got to know that
i was not completely blanked. I prepared oops, java, os, dsa but neither of them was asked to me.
When the interview got over, he asked me if I had any questions for him. Make sure u go through their
company website as it might help u to ask good questions to them. We were told that all the rounds will take
max 30 mins but my interview went for like 40 mins.
I was very unsure and I was not expecting to get selected for the next round. I even called my friend telling
--- PAGE 2 ---
him ki mera toh nhi hora because I was not able to answer some questions(till date I don't know whether the
answers I gave were actually correct or not). But, within 2 mins I got a call from the Barclays team to join
the meet. I thought they were going to tell ki u can go we are done but instead she told me that I was going
for the next round.

2. Round 2: HR (online) [ 4 out of 6 were selected for this round]

This was a pure Behavioral round. The interviewer didn't ask me typical HR questions, instead he told me
some values such as respect, challenges, stewardship etc and he directly asked me to point out and tell which
values I have followed or faced during working on the projects in teams. I started to explain my project and
then later I was trying to point out the values I have followed. But he told me that he didn't want to know the
project description, he just wanted to know the values I followed. Then he asked about any conflict that
might have happened between the team members. Basically this round was to see how fit you to work in a
corporate environment and how well you handle people. This round was entirely focused on values only. At
the end he asked me if I had any questions and that's all.
My hr round also went for like 40 mins.
The result was announced at around 7 pm and all 4 people were selected!

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. I would suggest you all to maintain 8.5+ cgpa for the safer side.

2. Also I would highly recommend you all to not lie in your resumes and you must know everything

you have mentioned in your resumes. Try giving your resume to chatgpt or gemini ai and ask to
generate questions based on it

3. Oops is a must to do. Also most companies prefer java so it would be great if u do oops in java. If

your preferred language is not java (like my preferred language was python) then try to do oops in
your preferred language as well as in java because they tend to ask and also expect u to know oops in
your preferred language.

4. DSA is a must to clear OAs and interviews as well (they might ask you to code in interviews).

Leetcode is best to practice dsa. U can follow strivers sheet but i didn't do that.

5. A tip for interviews- if u are not able to answer any question asked by the interviewer but u know

some related concept around the question then u must try to tell them that like u may say that "i don't
know about this but i can tell u about this" or take guesses so that they get to know that u r not totally
blank about the topic.

6. Avoid getting basic questions wrong in the interview. They don't expect you to know or answer every

question but you must not get the basic questions wrong or they might directly reject you.

7. Don't give robotic answers like as if tum rat k ya learn kar k aaye ho. Try to be natural

8. In the end i would say that placements are 60-70% based on luck. It may happen that even after

solving all questions in oa, u might not get selected. Just don't give up. Some companies do weird ass
shortlisting which may be beyond our imagination but just don't give up. I got into Barclays after
applying in almost 12-15 companies. Sometimes u may have breakdowns and u might feel dejected
but try to not think about it because most of the things are not in our hands and we can't do anything.
Remember God always has better plans for you.
Please feel free to reach out in case of any questions or doubts.
All the best!!

journey.prep:
- The entire interview was revolving around "what, when, where, and why" for each topic.

- Be honest with the interviewer and with your resume as well (as a fresher, they don't expect you to

know everything).

- In my case, Tech Round 1 was 80% DSA and Tech Round 2 was 80% Dev.

- During Dev rounds, it's a plus point to use fancy development terms in your answers, as the next

question may be related to them. However you should be familiar with these terms before using them.

- Having Internship experience helped me a lot they didn't focus on the project section of my resume.

- Thankfully I was not asked questions on aptitude and puzzles, as I was not well-prepared for them.

- Do prepare for Java because most companies work in Java.

- For DSA, Striver's A2Z is more than sufficient. First, try to understand the basics of all the concepts,

and then go in-depth into each one. In my case, I had solved 65% of the sheet, but I covered the
basics of all the topics. Most of the time, I repeated the videos multiple times if I felt that I hadn't
understood the concept properly.

- In an interview, your way of explanation and your approach to solv e the problem >>>> just providing

the correct ans. ( Focus on discussing multiple approach and explaining why some of them may not
work)

- Prepare for OOPs, DBMS, SQL, OS, and Dev concepts (including basic system design, as interviewers

often ask about basic system design nowadays, so don't neglect Dev).

- Participate in company hackathons it is a plus point during interviews.

If you have honestly put in the effort from your end, you will surely get what you deserve.
Best of luck!

journey.howSecured:
Following are rounds that occurred after applying:

1. Resume Shortlisting (63 students shortlisted for CDO Role)

2. Technical Round 1

3. Technical Round 2

4. HR Round

1.     [Written Test] [ 63 candidates appeared for this round]

In this round you will be given 1 hour(8:15 AM to 9:15 AM) to solve 1 MCQ, 2 Coding question, 1 SQL Query on
paper.

1. MCQ

2 MCQs were provided and we had to solve one of them

1) The first was based on the Left Shift (<<) operator

2) Second one was based on python scope variables

I solved the second one

2. Coding Question

We just had to write down function code in a format similar to LeetCode.

1. https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-k-sorted-lists/description/

I wrote optimal solution of this using priority queues.

2. https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-window-substring/description/

Solved using brute force approach

3.   SQL Query

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/sql-query-to-find-the-highest-salary-of-each-department/
I solved this query using 2 approach

1. Using GROUP BY with MAX()

2. Using ROW_NUMBER() Window Function

Tips: Try to write clear code. Avoid excessive edits or messy code (it should be easy for them to

understand and evaluate your approach, and also at each round your interviewer will have this paper in their
hand).
Write down comments at imp steps and proper naming for variables.
Keep a copy of your resume ready, as you will need to attach it with your answer paper during submission.

2. [Technical Round 1] [ 19 candidates were shortlisted for this round ]

This round lasted for more than an hour, and there were two interviewers present.

- The interview started by asking how many questions I solved in the test. They inquired about the

approach for each question, starting from the MCQs to the SQL query. For the first coding question,
they asked about the different approaches to solving the pr oblem, including their time and space
complexities, (I answered all brute, better and optimal) and why I ch oose the particular approach I
used. They also wanted to know why I selected a specific data structure and what would happen if the
conditions were changed. Additionally, they asked a few questions about linked lists, focusing on how
pointers worked in this question.

- They asked how a hash map works internally and what happens if there are collisions.

- They asked about sets and multisets, including when to use each, and the internal implementation of

priority queues in the C++ STL.

- I was asked to create a data structure similar to a hash map where the key is an element of an array,

and its value contains multiple indices where the element occurs in the array. I proposed using a linked
list for the value portion. The interviewer then asked how to retrieve the smallest and largest index
values from the linked list in less than O(n) time. I initially suggested a doubly linked list approach, but
noted that it would work for either the smallest or largest index, but not both efficiently. The interviewer
suggested to think for tree data structure instead of a linked list, which would reduce the time
complexity to O(log n). I was then asked to derive the time complexity mathematically  and plot the
graph for TC.

- They then asked further questions about Binary Search Trees.

- After this, he moved on to the second coding question and asked me to describe all the approaches

that could be applied to solve the problem, including their time and space complexities. I covered the
approaches from brute force to the optimal one using a sliding window. He then asked me to identify
various edge cases for the optimal approach.

- After this, he provided me with an array and asked me to find a particular element. I identified that it

was a rotated sorted array, so I suggested using binary search. He then asked me to explain condition
statements needed to write the code

- https://leetcode.com/problems/search-in-rotated-sorted-array/description/

- Further, they asked me about REST APIs what they are, the various types, methods, and the difference

between PUT and PATCH.

- They asked about abstraction, how it can be achieved, and the concepts of abstract classes and

interfaces, how to implement them and the differences between them.

- Difference between Having and where clause

- They asked about SQL and NoSQL databases, including what they are. They inquired about which

database to use for scaling, whether MySQL or MongoDB

- They also asked about indexing, database partitioning, and the criteria for partitioning a database.

- Lastly they asked about my role in the major project. I mentioned that I handled the entire web

development part while the rest of the AI/ML work was done by other team members.

They asked if I had any questions, so I inquired about the day-to-day work of the job role because I didn't
get a chance to attend the PPT.

3. HR Round

After being shortlisted from Technical Round 1, I was called for the HR round. This round lasted 20 to 25
minutes.
The questions asked were:

1. How was my day?

2. Where do I stay, how much time I spend in travelling, my daily schedule, and how I manage my time.

3. Work done during internships.

4. He asked me about hackathon s and  fortunately I had cleared Round 1 (Executive Summary) of the

Nomura KakushIn hackathon. He then asked about the solution we proposed for that hackathon. He
also inquired if I had participated in any other hackathons like this, to which I responded about Barclays
Hack-o-Hire. He then asked for details on the problem statement and the solution we proposed for
that hackathon.

5. How I was when I joined SPIT and how I have changed or developed since then.

6. He asked me to tell him something about myself that is not mentioned in my resume.

4. Technical Round 2

After the HR round, I was called for Technical Round 2. This round also lasted for more than an hour,
and there were two interviewers present, both of them are currently working under CDO at Nomura.

1. Tell me about yourself

2. What are the sorting algorithms and the time complexity (TC) of each of them?

3. Explain Merge Sort in detail.

4. Given a sorted array in ascending order, how would you sort it in descending order? Which algorithm

is most suitable for this, and which algorithm is the least suitable?

5. They gave me a SQL query that was an advanced version of the one provided during the coding test.

6. What are the pros and cons of using Arrays and Linked Lists? When should each be used? Provide a

real-life example.

7. In my resume, I had mentioned multiple AWS services, so they asked me about them, what work I did.

What is the AWS CLI?

8. What are REST APIs?

9. What is SOAP?

10. Different HTTP status code and their use?

11. What are WebSockets? When should they be used? Provide real-life examples. (The interviewer was

delving deeper into this, but then I told them that I have a basic understanding and haven't
implemented it yet, so they stopped asking further in-depth questions on this concept.)

12. Scenario-based question -> Given a 30 GB file, how would you find the frequency of words in it,

considering your system can process only 10 GB at a time? (I initially thought he was asking about the
concept of virtual memory, so I explained how high -end games like PUBG can run on 8 GB of RAM by
our OS, but he was looking for a different answer. He provided a hint about "Streams," which I caught
and explained how data streams can be used in such cases and how queries are performed on
streams.)

13.   What are MySQL and MongoDB? When should each be used? Provide real-life examples.

14. What is Polymorphism (including the meaning of the word)? What are its types, and provide a real -

life example.

15. What is Microservice architecture and Monolithic architecture?

16. When should Microservice architecture be used?

17. He gave me a scenario, "We usually see that the IRCTC app remains down. How would you solve this

problem?" I suggested deploying multiple backend applications and using load balancing. Then, he
asked me to explain this concept in detail.

18. Design a database schema for Amazon. I started by considering all types of users, but since it resulted

in a very large schema, he asked me to focus only on the user perspective (as it is already a bit difficult
question).

19. Lastly, they asked if I had any questions, so I inquired about the day-to-day work of the job role (same

question asked in Tech 1 also      ).

Total 13 students were selected: 3 for CDO, 8 for ITD, and 2 for the GM role.

recommended to have your webcam on and ask questions during the pre-placement talk.

2. Online Aptitude Test [155 (139 B.Tech + 16 MCA) students appeared this round]

This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine -
PARIKSHA. The test consisted of 60 questions, with 20 questions each in the verbal, analytical,
--- PAGE 2 ---
and quantitative sections, with no negative marking. The time limit was 60 minutes so timing is
the key here. The questions were of easy-medium difficulty.

questions first and then moving on to the quants as this section is time consuming.

about exact answer, i answered my views what i feel it can be

well.
This round lasted for about 45 minutes [dont know exactly], but it was not felt as burden. For
questions where I didn't know the answer, I explained my logic/thought-process and the
--- PAGE 3 ---

the areas you see am lacking at and areas that i am good at.

journey.prep:
1. Always believe in yourself. Even if you get nervous before the interviews begin; do not

overthink and over-prepare at the last minute.
Believe me, experiencing anxiety is normal and a part of the process. Be calm before the
rounds (trust me you will still feel anxious, but keeping it simple is the way to go).

2. Always answer questions honestly and confidently. If you know the logic behind a

problem; but don't know how to proceed with it; explain your thought process in a point-
wise manner to the interviewers. This will show your clarity. Keep a smile on your face
during the interviews in general (don't fake it though - it will make you seem nervous).
Maintain eye contact with the interviewers (don't stare at them; but periodically w hile
answering questions do so)
However, if you have no clue or have just heard about the problem; honestly tell the
interviewers that you don't know the answer (or that you are not familiar with the domain

- if it's a question out of your area of strength). Partially explaining a potent ially wrong

approach is detrimental.

3. Don't entirely focus on DSA. Yes, it is important and you will be asked about it in the

interviews (especially in Tech Round 2).
However, there's a high probability that you will be purely asked about your projects; and
more importantly SQL and DBMS questions in general (read the interview commonly
asked DBMS questions). I was not asked about any OS questions; but only if you get
additional time for preparation; you should prepare it as well (since they may ask it).
Also, if you have listed a NoSQL database as a skill in your resume; like MongoDB in my
case, prepare the basic queries (CRUD operations) and read about it briefly (MongoDB
ATLAS, clusters and so on…). I was asked about it in my Tech Round 2. Do this after you
have prepared DSA and DBMS.

4. Regarding the OA (Online Assessment); try attempting as many questions as possible. We

had 60 questions (20 Math, 20 Verbal, 20 Analytical). Try to attempt at least 40 questions
in 40-45 mins. It's not necessary to attempt every question correctly. I properly attempted
about 40-45 in 50 mins.
If and only if; there is no negative marking (which will most likely be the case) try to take
an estimated guess for the remaining questions (narrow down the options & then guess); if
you believe estimation is taking time, blindly guess the answers (you still have a 1/4 chance
of getting it right).

5. Be extremely thorough with the projects listed in your resume. It's not necessary to list 4 -

5 projects. Even listing 2 -3 of your best projects can create a great impression on the
interviewers. In my case; the 3 projects that I had listed were mainly ML/DL  based with
data analytics incorporated (Tableau); with a single project being that of web development
(backend - Django).
Limit the projects mainly to your strongest domain. But have at least 1 project from a
different domain (since they will look for variety as well). Mention your contribution to
each project. It's better to mention it in the resume itself (in 2 -3 lines). Be genuine with
your answers. Elaborate upon the skills that you applied in the project. Only mention those
skills which you genuinely have (above 50 % of the knowledge). If you don't have any real
experience in the skill that you have mentioned; better to leave it out of the resume.

6. Lastly, during any round (be it technical/HR/GD) be the driving force of the interview. It's

not necessary to completely take over and start explaining everything in one go. Be
proactive and show that you are passionate about what you are doing; and that you really
would like to make a positive impact on the company.
Answer every question confidently and concisely. But do not deliberately give short
incomplete answers and wait for follow -up questions. This will show the interviewer that
you do not like to lead from the front and wait for other people to push you around . Give
answers; which you believe will properly be able to explain the interviewer's question.

Resources:

1. Do DSA from Striver (TakeUForward). Simply the best and clearest DSA course that I

have come across. (Instead of subscribing to TUF+; you can watch his YouTube playlists).
Practice the DSA questions on leetcode (mainly the top interview 150); & if time permits
do some problems from - codingNinjas/GFG and so on … (Practice his SDE sheet; or
whatever sheet you feel comfortable with.)

2. Prepare theory questions for DBMS (and if time permits OS - not necessary in general)

from InterviewBit (top 75 most commonly asked questions). You may use any other
website to do so; I found InterviewBit to be well-organized.  You can read from GFG as
well (although I find it relatively more time-consuming).

3. For quick SQL revision; read the entire syntax overview on W3Schools (I prefer keeping

it simple and just doing it for MySQL). Do as many problems of the Leetcode SQL 50 as
possible for practice.

4. Practice puzzles from GFG (mainly) and coding ninjas (as an additional resource; if time

permits). You will almost certainly be asked to solve at least one puzzle during your
interview rounds.
.

5. If time permits, watch Gaurav Sen's system design playlist on YouTube. Chances of

questions related to designing apps are very slim; but you may get some conceptual
questions (like vertical/horizontal scaling and so on…)

If you have any questions for me, you can connect with me & ask; on LinkedIn or by Mail.
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jay-nadkarni-232714172/
Mail: jayvnadkarni@gmail.com

That's it from my side.
ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR PLACEMENTS!!!

1st August, 2024 - Pre-Placement Talk (PPT)

Pre-Placement Talk for Nomura was held online on 1/8/2024. Pay attention during the PPT and
take note of the roles and responsibilities that are offered. After this, your resumes will be
collected; and your shortlisting for the OA will happen based on your  resume (Use FlowCV or
LaTex to make your resume).

1. Online Assessment (OA) [155 students]

After my resume was shortlisted; I gave the OA. This was a pure aptitude test (no coding questions
were asked). I had 60 mins to answer 60 questions. There were 3 sections: quantitative (math),
verbal and analytical (logic), each with 20 questions.

You can prepare for these questions from IndiaBix aptitude questions  or even solve basic GRE
questions (even if you don't intend to take the exam) since the format is very similar. In my case;
I did the latter.

I aimed to attempt as many questions as possible correctly in 45 minutes. It's practically impossible
to attempt all 60 properly (let alone get all correct) within this time.

I completed 40 -45 questions within 45 mins; after which I spent the remaining time making
estimated guesses for the remaining questions. Finally, I attempted 59 questions out of 60 (time
ran out while I was attempting the 60th). But you should try to attempt all the questions (if and
only if there is no negative marking).

My advice would be: solve the easiest questions first (those which have formulaic/direct answers);
then go to the medium ones (which click for you; but might take some time to solve) & approach
the hard questions (questions in which you have to think about the approach of solving or
extremely lengthy questions in general). You can take guesses for the hard ones at the end (if you
couldn't solve them) but try to crack the easy and medium ones.

Do not go section-wise; since you may leave out easy & medium questions of the other sections
while attempting the hard questions of your current section.

32 candidates were selected for the interview round for the ITD role and I was happy to be
one of them.

- I was shortlisted for both the ITD role (based on my OA results); and the GM role

as well (based on my resume). [Go directly to 'For ITD Role' if you just want to
know about it]

For GM (global markets) Role-

2. Group Discussion Round [40 Students]

5 groups of 10 students were formed. Our topic was Cryptocurrency - whether it was good or bad.
We were given 5 mins to prepare (I jotted down important points on a piece of paper).
At the start, everyone had to introduce themselves and the topic. I explained the topic at hand; &
what we might discuss today.
Then the full-fledged discussion started. I made  5-6 valid points. Referenced recent events
regarding the topic as well. Countered the arguments of my peers; which I thought were a bit
superfluous. Encouraged participation by encouraging my peers to continue from where I left off.
Spoke about both the pros and cons of Blockchain as a whole (mentioning Ethereum and Bitcoin-
specific points as well) - but not in the same entry (basically speaking about the pros & cons; but
during different entries with valid p oints). Maintained eye contact with my peers and had a
confident body posture.
Finally, everyone had to conclude. Summarized the discussion; told what issues we might have
missed during the discussion ( NFTs, Metaverse…). I concluded by saying; that overall, it was a
great discussion.
The total duration was 15 -20 minutes. 4 students from my group (including me) were
shortlisted for the next round.

3. Technical Round 1 [16 students]

There was a single interviewer; who greeted me. He asked me to introduce myself and what my
interests were. I properly introduced myself and told him about my passion for data analysis and
machine learning.

He then asked me questions regarding my projects (I explained to him about all 3 of my listed
projects; and my contributions in them).

My projects (for those who wish to know)-

- Anomaly Detection System (DetectX) - Made during Aeravat ML Hackathon

- Self-Driving Car in a Simulated Environment (using neural networks):  ongoing project (at

the time) for the college major project

- Food Delivery Website made using React and Django (Team Project). [Personally worked

on creating the admin dashboard and models -> as part of the backend]

He asked me about the difficulties that I faced in these projects and how I overcame them. Later,
he asked me some general questions like:

- Tell me about a time when you experienced failure. How did you cope with it? (told them about

my JEE results and my motivation to do better and learn from them)

- What mistake would you like to avoid that you might have made during a project of yours? Why?

(I explained it honestly. This depends from person to person)

Finally, he asked me some language-specific questions (after I told him that Python is my primary
prog. language):

- Difference between / and // in python (wrt division).

- What is monkey patching in Python?

(I was unable to answer this; basically, it means re-assigning the method inside a class as
another function outside it; so that the next time the class method is called; the modified
function gets called.)

- What is the init method in Python (in classes)? (Constructor. Explain the self keyword as

well here)

- How will you remove duplicates from an array and preserve the order?

(This was a DSA question. Since order needs to be preserved; we cannot directly use set
OR sort the array and then use it for loops… So I told him that I would use a dictionary/hash
map and explained my code properly, given below)

def remove_duplicates(arr):
seen = {}
result = []
for elem in arr:
if elem not in seen:
seen[elem] = True
result.append(elem)
return result

Later he asked me whether I had any questions for him.
(I asked him about the career growth opportunities at Nomura for a data-oriented person like me).

The total duration was 30-35 minutes. 6 students were selected for the next round, and I

4. Technical Round 2 [6 students]

There was a panel of 2 interviewers this time. Again, I was asked to introduce myself and elaborate
upon my projects. After doing so they started with the DSA and SQL questions:

- There is a key 'x' in a nested hash -map/dictionary at some unknown depth. Return the

value associated with that key. I gave the following solution (used yield => since there
might be multiple x keys (in different dicts))

def gen_dict_extract(var, key):
if isinstance(var, dict):
for k, v in var. items():
if k == key:
yield v
if isinstance(v, (dict, list)):
yield from gen_dict_extract(v, key)
elif isinstance(var, list):
for d in var:
yield from gen_dict_extract(d, key)

- What happens when the root of a BST is deleted?

(replace the root with either its inorder successor (smallest/leftmost node of the right
subtree)
or in order predecessor (largest/rightmost node of the left subtree))

- Finally, I was given a puzzle - Find the 3 fastest Horses. I was able to solve it properly.

Refer to solution: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/puzzle-9-find-the-fastest-3-horses/

Then they asked me if I had any questions. I asked them what exactly was expected from interns
at the GM role; and how is the work environment at Nomura.

The total duration was 30-40 minutes. The final selection for the GM role was going to
occur after TR2 and HR rounds were over (at once).

5. HR Round [6 students]

The HR interviewer was very friendly and relaxed. She told me to calm down and asked me
standard HR questions:

-  Introduction + Family Background

- What are my strengths and weaknesses?

- Where do I see myself in 5 years?

- How would I fit in at Nomura?

- How flexible and adaptable am I at learning new things?

- Tell me about when you experienced failure and how you overcame it.

Then she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked her about the overall work experience and
culture at Nomura. Additionally, I asked her about the variety of different people (from different
states/countries) that I would get to meet at Nomura.

The total duration was 15-20 minutes. My HR interview went very well. However, there
were only 2 vacancies for the GM role; and I was more suited for development; so in the
end I was selected for the ITD role.

2 students were finally selected for the GM roles.

For ITD (info tech div) Role- (for which I was shortlisted)

2.   Technical Round 1 [32 students]

There was a panel of 2 interviewers. They told me to introduce myself and got acquainted with my
areas of strength - Machine Learning, Data Science and Analytics in general. They asked me
questions regarding my projects thoroughly, like-

- What is your best project? Why is it so?

- What did you learn from this project? How did you work within a team (for the team

projects) and what you could have done better?

- Why was this model (for ML) preferable to you? Why not the others? …

Do thorough research and reading on your projects , and you will be able to answer the above
questions with ease.

Then I was asked language-specific questions in depth. I had told them that Python was my main
programming language in general - for DSA, ML, and backend (Django).

- They asked me about an iterator in Python and how to define it. He then asked me to explain

how it works; and how it is different from using loops. I explained it properly while giving
examples having the correct syntax. (iter -> keyword for iterator; next -> used to iterate
through the iterator)

- They asked me about what decorators (@decorator_name basically in Python) are and how

to define them. Upon explaining what they were; they asked me to manually write a
decorator function to be applied to another function. I was able to do so (since my Python
skills were very good).

- I was asked about generators and how to define them. (Basically , use the yield keyword

instead of return). They asked me about its advantages - we can use multiple yield
statements at the same level (not true for return); and that such functionality can enable
returning multiple things (useful for sequences) which is n ot possible with the return
keyword.

He then asked me to rate myself in Python proficiency: I rated myself 9/10.

Some more questions included-

- Defining normalization and explaining the different normal forms (I told them from 1NF

to 5NF but practically speaking telling till BCNF is fine)

- I was asked to explain NoSQL databases - and which one I used (MongoDB). They asked

me why I preferred it (good extensive documentation; MongoDB ATLAS enables cross -
connecting clusters with ease across the internet; most mainstream and in-demand NoSQL
db with good community support).
I was asked to write/explain the basic CRUD operations for MongoDB (insertOne,
insertMany, find, findbyID, updateOne, updateMany, deleteOne, deleteMany and so on…)

- Finally they asked me a basic SQL query (write a SQL query to find the employees who

have a salary greater than the average salary in their department.) I wrote it in MySQL
syntax.

SELECT e1.*
FROM employees e1
JOIN (
SELECT department, AVG(salary) as avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
) e2 ON e1.department = e2.department
WHERE e1.salary > e2.avg_salary

(Basically, a combination of self-join and group by)

Then they asked me if I had any questions for them. I asked 2 (one for each panellist)-

- What is the overall work culture at Nomura? How good is the team bonding?

- What advice would you give to a data enthusiast like me? What is the scope for data -

centric interns at Nomura?

- Finally, I was given a puzzle.

Form 10 from 1,1,5,8 using any of the operations: +,-,*,/ (Use all the digits in any order at least
once)

No one was able to answer this puzzle (including me); from those who were given to solve
this. The interviewers themselves said that it was a very hard puzzle; after seeing my thought
process and that I was going in the right direction.

Solution: 8 ÷ (1 - 1 ÷ 5) = 10
Refer this: https://mindyourdecisions.com/blog/2015/09/20/viral-math-problem-from-
google-can-you-make-10-from-the-numbers-1-1-5-and-8/

The total duration was 40-45 minutes. 16 were selected for the next round, and I was

3.    Technical Round 2 + HR [16 students]

There were 2 panelists again. They asked me to introduce myself and what my strengths were.
Additionally, since both the rounds were combined I was asked a lot of non-tech general questions
(HR-related) as well; like:-

- What are your hobbies? How did you pursue this hobby?

(I told them about sports - Cricket & Table Tennis; and mentioned Chess (specifically 1
min Bullet chess) - which helped me improve my concentration and patience)

- Since I was very experienced in ML/DL; they asked me why I wanted to work at Nomura.

Wouldn't my skills be better suited to big tech companies (MAANG)?
(I told them; that my passion  was for working with data; and identifying the trends and
patterns in it; along with proper analysis. It doesn't matter to me what type of data it was.
Additionally, I told them about my interest in the stock market (mentioned to them about
having a Zerodha trading account , and learning more about the stock market through the
Zerodha varsity course))

They also asked me about my projects in depth. (Similar to TR1). I was able to answer most of the
questions. However, here they gave me slightly negative feedback; that I elaborated excessively
upon my answers; leaving no room for follow-up questions. I took this feedback positively; and
told them that I would be more concise from here on.

Then they moved on to the technical questions (mainly DSA)-

- How to check if a string is a palindrome or not without using any loops or inbuilt functions?

A combination of 2 pointer and recursion.

def is_palindrome(s, i=0, j=None):
if j is None:
j = len(s) - 1 - i
if i >= j:
return True
if s[i] != s[j]:
return False
return is_palindrome(s, i + 1, j - 1)

- They asked me what was Dijkstra's algorithm; and then told me to write the basic code for

finding the minimum distance using it (even pseudocode is fine).

# Graph is the form of adjacency linked list; also use priority queue (using heap)
Dijkstra(Graph, Start):
Dist = infinity for all nodes
Dist[Start] = 0
Queue = all nodes
while Queue is not empty:
Node = extract min from Queue
for Neighbor of Node:
if Dist[Node] + Weight(Node, Neighbor) < Dist[Neighbor]:
Dist[Neighbor] = Dist[Node] + Weight(Node, Neighbor)
Previous[Neighbor] = Node
return Dist

- I was asked about a challenging problem that I solved and how did I approach it?

(I told them about cherry pickup-II (and explained the problem properly). I deliberately chose
a very hard 3D DP problem since I wanted to showcase my problem-solving ability. I gave
them the memoization solution (after explaining the recursion first); but told them that further
slight space optimizations such as tabulation; and then space optimized tabulation are possible.
)

def cherryPickup(grid):
# Define a helper function to perform dynamic programming recursion
def _cherryPickup(row, col1, col2):
# Out of bounds check
if col1 < 0 or col1 >= n or col2 < 0 or col2 >= n:
return float("-inf")

# Memoization check
if dp[row][col1][col2] != -1:
return dp[row][col1][col2]

# Base case: last row
if row == m - 1:
if col1 == col2:
# Collect one cherry
return grid[row][col1]
else:
# Collect two cherries
return grid[row][col1] + grid[row][col2]

# Recursive case
max_s = 0
for d1 in range(-1, 2):
for d2 in range(-1, 2):
# Calculate the maximum number of cherries that can be collected
if col1 == col2:
max_s = max(max_s, grid[row][col1]
+ _cherryPickup(row + 1, col1 + d1, col2 + d2))
else:
max_s = max(max_s, grid[row][col1] + grid[row][col2] +
_cherryPickup(row + 1, col1 + d1, col2 + d2))

# Memoize the result
dp[row][col1][col2] = max_s
return max_s

Finally, they asked me some SQL questions:

- What are indexes? What are the main types? (clustered and non-clustered)

- Do you know about window functions in MySQL? Give the general format (you can give

any specific example - like rank or dense_rank)

SELECT window_function(column) OVER (
PARTITION BY partition_expression
ORDER BY order_expression
Frame_specification # is not necessary to mention this...
) AS alias

After this, the interviewers were impressed with my knowledge and abilities. They had a slight
criticism at the end though (that I needed to broaden my skill set in various domains , not just
ML/DL. Upon this I told them that I had been undertaking various courses - such as Android App

They asked if I had any questions for them. I asked the following question:

viz.? What will I learn in this role?

1. Pre-placement talk

This was an online round. We were briefed about the company, its values and the roles they offered
There were 3 roles available for us in 3 different divisions, ITD, GM and CDO. It is recommended to
have your webcam on and ask questions during the pre-placement talk.

2. Online Aptitude Test [155 (139 B.Tech + 16 MCA) students appeared for this round]

This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA.
The test consisted of 60 questions, with 20 questions each in the verbal, analytical, and quantitative
sections, with no negative marking. The time limit was 60 minutes so timing is the key here. The
questions were of easy-medium difficulty. IndiaBix is a great resource for practicing. I'd recommend
solving the verbal and analytical questions first and then moving on to the quants as this section is time
consuming.
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Technical Interview 1[32 (22 B.Tech + 10 MCA) students were shortlisted for the ITD Role]

This round started at around 10 am. My interviewer was the Assistant Vice President at Nomura. I was
asked to introduce myself, then the interviewer went through my resume and asked me to explain any
project that I found interesting. I explained about a game that I had developed in Java in one of the
hackathons at SPIT and he was impressed. He went on to ask SQL questions based on normalisation,
joins and indexing. He then moved on to Java and some basic questions on DSA & OOPS like
polymorphism, hashmap, hashset, What would be the best data structure if you want to insert an element
between a list? etc. I was more comfortable with C++ but that was not an issue as the interviewer was
okay with it. He asked me to write java code on method overriding and followed up with some questions
on it. This round lasted for 30 minutes only, I was able to answer almost all the questions. For questions
where I didn't know the answer, I explained my logic and the interviewer was satisfied with it. He asked
if I had any questions from him and I asked him about his tech-stack and if he had any feedback for me.
Overall this round was to test my basics in Java and SQL.

4. Technical Interview 2 [16 (12 B.Tech + 4 MCA) students were shortlisted for this round]

This round started at around 1.30 pm. There were 2 interviewers in each panel for this round. I was
immediately called for the interview after lunch. I greeted the interviewers first and asked them about
their day and they asked me the same. They went through my resume and asked me detailed questions
about the technical skills that I had mentioned in the resume. I was asked questions about SQL and Java
again, this time in more detail. What would be the output of: select * from tablel, table2? How many
rows would be in the output for certain values if full outer join is used? I was asked if I was comfortable
with Linux, AWS and Python. None of these were mentioned in my resume but I was able to answer
basic questions based on these topics. Further, they asked a lot of questions on DevOps as I had
mentioned it in my resume. The questions were: How did you build a Jenkins pipeline? Why did you
choose maven over gradle? How did you use Selenium for testing? Can you create multiple containers
for one application? This was followed with some basic questions on git commands. They asked
questions based on collections in java and then data structures in C++ as I was more comfortable with
that. Finally, I was asked some basic OOPS questions. The interviewers then moved on to HR questions
which was a little unexpected but it worked out well as we had a great discussion about our daily
schedules, the blue-screen error on windows etc. This discussion lasted for more than 10 minutes and I
was confident that I did well! They had a very positive feedback and asked me to get comfortable with
Linux as that's a must in most corporate offices. This round lasted for around 45 mins.

5. HR Round [8 (6 B.Tech + 2 MCA) students were shortlisted for this round]

This round started 10 minutes after my second technical interview ended. She asked me to introduce
myself with something about myself that I had not mentioned in my resume. I was asked scenario based
questions like: What would you do if your teammates are not following deadlines and pushed the work
on you? What would you do if you get an error in your code that would impact the project heavily in the
--- PAGE 3 ---
future? etc. She also asked me about my hobbies and what I knew about Nomura. This round ended on a
positive note.
The results were declared at 5.30 pm and 8 students (6 B.Tech + 2 MCA) were selected for this role.

[ 4 Rounds ]

1.     [Aptitude Test]

This test consisted of 3 sections :
a) English Proficiency
b) Logical Reasoning
c) Quants
It was an online test.
When preparing for an aptitude test like the one you're about to take, it's crucial to understand the test
structure and strategize accordingly. The test consists of 60 questions to be completed within 60 minutes,
giving you only one minute per question on average.
  Quantitative Aptitude and Logical Reasoning: The questions in these sections range from easy to
medium difficulty. While they may not be overly challenging, they can be tricky and time-consuming,
especially if you get bogged down in calculations or overthink the logic puzzles. The key here is to
practice extensively (GFG & IndiaBix) so that you can quickly recognize the types of problems and
solve them efficiently.
  English Proficiency: This section includes lengthy paragraph-based questions, which typically test
your reading comprehension, vocabulary, and ability to interpret and analyze text. These questions can
be particularly time-consuming, so it's important to read the passage swiftly but carefully. Look for key
information that will help you answer the questions without needing to re-read the entire passage.

2. [Technical Round 1]

I was interviewed by the Assistant Vice President of ITD at Nomura. The round began with the most
common question: "Walk me through your resume." It's important to note that while answering this
question, you are not expected to explain every line of your resume in detail. The interviewer is
primarily interested in a brief overview of your skills, projects, and professional experience (if any).
The interviewer was quite friendly and conducted the interview more like a conversation rather than a
Q&A session. Regarding the technical aspects, I, along with other candidates, was mainly asked
fundamental questions on operating systems, OOPs, Python, and one DSA question (primarily focused
on sorting algorithms and their time complexity). You can also expect a guesstimate question.
Additionally, I was asked two puzzle questions:

1. Three bulbs and three switches.

2. Nine marbles, out of which eight marbles weigh the same. How do you find the odd one out with

the minimum number of comparisons?
There were also questions on RAM and ROM (SSD, HDD), as well as a few fundamental questions
about the roles of an investment bank and the basics of finance. It's beneficial to have some knowledge
in these areas.
The interview lasted around 45 minutes. At the end, we were given the opportunity to ask the
interviewer a question. Since I knew who was going to interview me, I had already researched his role
on LinkedIn. He specialized in testing and CI/CD, so I asked him questions related to these concepts.
I was shortlisted after this round, along with 15 other candidates, making a total of 16 candidates who
were shortlisted.

3. [Technical Round 2]

I was interviewed by two senior associates from Nomura. The first question they asked was about my
industrial internship. When answering this question, it's important to use the WHY, WHEN, & WHAT
format. This round was quite grilling, and the interviewers were somewhat intimidating. However, their
main objective was to assess my confidence and body language while responding to their questions.
They might interrupt you with another question while you're answering the previous one, but don't worry
if this happens--it's just a test of your temperament and domain knowledge.
Regarding the technical questions, I was asked a couple of DSA problems:

1. A 2-D matrix question where I had to find the largest number that can be constructed by

traversing from the first row to the bottom row, which can be solved using the graph concept of
DFS traversal.

2. A string anagram question.

Both of these questions are available on LeetCode. I initially provided a brute-force approach, explained
the time complexity, and validated my solution with the test cases they provided. I was also asked to
optimize the time complexity, which I successfully did for both questions, and the interviewers were
quite satisfied with my solutions and their efficiencies.
Since I had mentioned machine learning and visualization on my resume, they asked me about
Statistical Analysis. Specifically, they asked me to explain the difference between mean and average.
They also questioned me about AP (Arithmetic Progression) and GP (Geometric Progression) and
presented me with a puzzle based on these two series. Additionally, they tested my knowledge of core
Java, particularly threads and OOPs concepts.

This round lasted around 50 minutes, and I was shortlisted for the HR round.

4. [HR]

You can expect this round to be more of a Techno-HR interview rather than just typical HR questions. I
was primarily asked about my projects, particularly the difficult situations I encountered and how I
resolved those challenges. Situational-based questions were also a key part of the interview (you can
refer to IndiaBix for HR questions).
During this round, it's essential to be completely yourself. While it's good to have a structured approach
to answering HR questions, make sure your responses don't sound too rehearsed or idealistic. Keep your
answers specific and to the point--avoid over-elaboration.
Finally, after this round, 8 people, including myself, were selected.

Process Date:

(All the processes were offline at the college)

- 11th July (PPT + OA)

- 12th July (2 Technical Rounds + 1 Hiring Manager Round)

Online Assessment/Coding Round [291 students appeared]:
This round was conducted on DoSelect platform. Questions: 4, Time: 90mins

1. Given an array, print the number of subarrays where XOR of all elements in the subarray, should

have an even number of divisors.
Eg. arr = [1 2 3]
Output: 3
Subarray [1, 2] has XOR value 3 (1, 3 are the divisors)
Subarray [2] has XOR value 2 (1, 2 are the divisors)
Subarray [3] has XOR value 3 (1, 3 are the divisors)

2. Given an array, print the lexicographically smallest array possible by swapping elements any number

of times but you can only swap 2 elements with each other if their XOR is strictly less than 4.
Eg. arr = [5, 2, 1, 4]
Output: [4, 1, 2, 5]
You can only swap (1, 2) and (4, 5) among themselves
--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Given a binary string of length 'n', and 'q' queries having ranges L to R(1 based indexed and both

are inclusive). For every query, you have to sort the elements in the range L to R on the original
string to obtain a new string. Output the number of unique strings that would be obtained after all q
queries.
Eg. s = "11001»
Queries = [(2, 4), (3, 4), (3, 5)]
Output: 2
First query will result in : 10011
Second query will result in : 11001
Third query will result in : 11001

4. Given a directed graph and q queries related to it. The queries could be of 3 types. Add a dependency

(add edge A->B), remove a dependency (remove edge(A->B), query for checking a transitive
dependency (is there any we could reach B from A).
All the problems were solvable with brute-force approach. Most of the people who were shortlisted solved 2
problems completely and the other 2 partially. The total test was worth 400 points (each problem was worth
100 points, partial scoring was also counted), and your final score would be considered out of 400. Try to
read every problem first and attempt easier ones first. Keep trying to solve it till the last minute, wrong
submission doesn't have any penalty.

1. Technical Round 1[30 students]

There were two interviewers for my panel in this round. It started with the standard "Tell me about yourself"
question. I mentioned that I enjoy working on the backend, and they asked me why. Based on my answer,
they then asked me to describe a situation where I scaled or optimized a backend system.
The first technical question was Number of Flowers in Full Bloom - LeetCode. I initially explained the brute
force approach, then moved on to the difference array technique. They asked if we could optimize the space
complexity. For that, I suggested a different approach using sorting and two-pointers. Both approaches had
trade-offs in terms of time or space complexity. They then asked me to write the code for one of the
approaches on paper.
The second question was Lexicographically Kth smallest way to reach given coordinate from origin -
GeeksforGeeks. At first, I approached the problem using mathematical observation but it seemed too
complicated, and then I suggested that we keep generating the next permutation of the string k times but that
also had very bad time complexity. After seeing me struggle they gave me a hint, and I was able to figure
out the correct approach. I did a dry run on a test case, but as time was running out, they didn't ask me to
write the code for this one.
--- PAGE 3 ---
Tip: Even if you are not sure of your approach share it with them, they will help you point in the right
direction. Keep trying till the end maybe you figure out the approach at the last minute it matters a lot

2. Technical Round 2[13 students] (there were 3 of us whose round 2 happened after HM round)

In this interview round, there was one interviewer. First, he asked about the online assessment (OA) and my
day. Then he went straight to the first question: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully
Traversable - LeetCode. I mentioned that type 3 edges are always preferable. I explained my approach of
creating a minimum spanning tree using disjoint sets. He asked about the time complexity of the find_parent
function in a disjoint set union. I said it would be O(n), but with memoization, it could be reduced to O(1)
amortised time complexity. However, he pointed out that we should still consider the worst-case time
complexity as O(n). Then, I was asked to write the code on paper.
Next, he asked the second question:
"Given an N*M matrix initially set to 0 (where 0 indicates land and 1 indicates water), each day, a piece of
land at some (i, )) will turn into water. Given this input and the number of rows and columns, we need to
find the last day on which we could still reach the last row from the top row."
Since the previous question was about disjoint set union (DSU), my thoughts were making me think about a
solution using a similar approach. I observed that we could flip the problem to find the first day a river
would be formed; the day before that would be our answer. I explained my DSU solution, which had a time
complexity of O(N^2 * M^2) in the worst case. He asked if we could improve the time complexity and
hinted not to invert the problem and to optimize how we add water each day. I realized the approach should
involve binary search. After a few minutes of thinking, I provided a BFS + binary search approach with a
time complexity of ON * M * log(N * M)). The round ended with me asking him two questions.

3. Hiring Manager Round [9 students]

This round lasted over an hour, and the interviewer was an Engineering Manager at PhonePe. On the way to
the interview room, we had a brief chat about where I live and other small talk. The focus of this round was
mainly on my resume. It began with the usual "Tell me about yourself" question, followed by a detailed
discussion about my internships and projects. The questions were not very technical; they were more about
how I would implement additional use cases.
He asked about my final year project. I explained that it was only halfway completed, which is why it wasn't
on my resume. I described what was done so far and our plans for the next phase. He followed up by asking
how the project could be adapted for use at PhonePe and asked for a basic system overview. He then gave
me feedback on how to proceed in the next phase.
Next, he asked some behavioural questions. I initially didn't realize they were non-technical and should be
answered accordingly, so don't make this mistake. He asked what I would do in my first three months at a
new company and how I would handle a situation where the code I'm trying to understand is written by
--- PAGE 4 ---
someone who is very busy. He also asked about a situation where I had any conflicts with friends or
teammates.
He then asked if I had explored PhonePe app. I said I had only used it for making payments and hadn't
explored other features. He asked me to explain the process flow for scanning and making a payment to a
merchant's QR code and encouraged me to use paper if needed. I gave a brief explanation of what I thought
happened behind the scenes but didn't draw a proper architecture or process flow.
At the end, I asked him a few questions. Taking the stairs to the fourth floor had left me out of breath and
made me nervous initially, but the interviewer was very friendly and made me feel comfortable.
6 students received the offer (Intership+FTE).

it down into smaller problems and keep sharing your ideas with the interviewer.

a. Be transparent while answering the questions (avoiding unnecessary details)
b. They want to assess your attitude and behaviour in this round
c. Try to show that you are passionate about what you do and always keen to learn

4. Remember, it's not over until it is, so keep trying until the end, even if you least expect things to go

your way.

Process Dates:

- 11th June (Pre-placement Talks + Online Assessment (DoSelect)

- 12th June (Interview Rounds - 2 Technical Rounds, HR Round)

Coding Round:

- 90 Minutes - 4 Questions (Almost 300 students appeared for this test)

1. Given an array, return the number of subarrays where xor of all elements in the

subarray, should have an even number of divisors.

2. Output the lexicographically smallest array, where you can perform array

swapping operation (any number of times) on index i, j (i<j) where arrli]^arri] < 4.

3. Given a binary string of length 'n', and 'q' queries having ranges I to r. For every

query, you have to sort the elements in the range I to r on the original string to
obtain a new string. Output the number of unique strings that would be obtained
after all q queries.

4. Given a directed graph and q queries related to it. The queries could be of 3

types. Add a dependency, remove a dependency, query for checking a transitive
dependency.
I was able to solve the first 2 questions completely and partially solved the third
question. Expertise in problem solving is required to clear this round.
30 students were shortlisted for the interviews on the next day.
Round - 1 (Technical Round) | 30 Students
There were 15 panels that were going on simultaneously for Round - 1
interviews.
The round started with the panelist introducing himself, and he explained about his work
at PhonePe. I was curious about it so I asked him a few questions related to it. The
interviewer then asked me for my introduction. In my introduction I mentioned that I was
--- PAGE 2 ---
a specialist on codeforces and then we had a discussion on codeforces rounds. We
then started with the questions.

1. Given n ranges of time period (start day and end day) during which a flower

blossoms in a garden, followed by q queries, where i-th query represents the day
on which a person would come to the garden. The answer to the i-th query is the
total number of flowers blossomed during those days.
Almost immediately, I gave him the brute force approach of it, moving to the
optimal prefix summation technique. He then increased the constraints of the
ranges to 1e9, so we won't have an array that huge. Since I had solved some
similar range type questions on CSES, I had some intuitions for a better
approach. During the discussion to improvise time complexity even further I
suggested a segment tree approach, to which he said that would work with the
given time complexity constraints but to think of another approach that wouldn't
use a complex data structure. Using a hint I was able to solve this question, and I
was asked to write the complete code of it on paper.

2. Given a matrix of MxN size, we can move to right or down, we want to reach

some arbitrary point (x,y) and for every move we append H for right or V for down
in a string. Of all the possible strings, we want to give the k-th lexicographically
smallest string. He was expecting a mathematical solution to it rather than a
graph. Took a few hints to reach the mathematical solution from a graph based
approach. There wasn't enough time left to write the code for this question but
the interviewer was satisfied with our discussion of both the questions.
I asked him a few questions that I was curious about after the pre-placement talk. 14
students were shortlisted after round.
Round - 2 (Technical Round) [ 14 students ]

- All the 14 selected candidates were being interviewed simultaneously.

There were 2 interviewers in my panel. The round started with both of them introducing
themselves. The interviewers clarified in the beginning that they expect me to write code
of both the questions on paper and take minimum hints for the 2 questions that they
would ask me. (But I'm guessing that it was just to try and put me under some pressure
situation even before giving me the problems)

1. Given a grid of NxM size, initially all the boxes would be filled with 0, and another

array of pair of integers which mention that on i-th day, (x,y) box would be
flooded with water (can be represented with 1, and 0 would mean that the grid
isn't flooded). Find the maximum 'i for which I can travel from top to bottom (one
--- PAGE 3 ---
can move in all 4 directions) and I can only step on non-flooded grid at a time. At
first I gave them a tricky, new approach, to which they both were quite intrigued
and all 3 of us were working on some test case on which my approach would fail.
Eventually I could come with a test case that my solution would fail on. And then I
asked for a hint, to which he told me that a monotonic function is being
developed on the days array. I was able to gather from this hint that it is a binary
search solution. I then gave him the binary search + bfs solution to it. We
discussed the time complexity of it and I wrote the code for it on paper.

2. We are given a graph and it consists of 3 types of edges, type -1 edge can only

be traversed by alex, type -2 edges can only be traversed by bob and type -3
edges can be traversed by both of them. So how many maximum edges can be
removed so both of them are able to traverse all vertices present in the graph. In
almost no time I could come up with the optimal approach to solve this problem
using 2 DSU's. I explained to them the structure of a DSU. This was the optimal
approach they were expecting. They made me write the code for this problem
first assuming that I have the DSU class implemented, and after I wrote the code
for this, they asked me to implement the DSU class. I wrote all the codes on
paper.
By the end of this interview, I was too exhausted and thirsty so I didn't ask them any
questions, but in both the technical rounds I had some amazing conversations with the
panelists (so basically it became fine for me to not ask any question I believe XD). 9
people cleared this round (of which 3 of us had our HM round taken before round - 2
because they wanted to optimize the interview process, I was one of them).
Round - 3 (HM Round) | 9 students ]
I was called for this round right after my round - 1 interviews. Going to the room I was
expecting a technical round. But it was only after I sat down I got to know this was a HM
Round. The interviewer started reading my resume. And asked me questions on
everything and anything that I had written in it. He asked me questions related to my
projects, on what was my learning, or if something that could be added. He asked me a
few questions related to my competitive programming skills, like why giving more
contests on these platforms makes me a better engineer and not just a better coder. He
asked me questions relating to my experience and work in CSI-SPIT. He asked me a
few behavioral questions and gave a few situations and how I would respond to those.
For all such situations he also wanted me to give some personal examples. He asked
me if I had used the PhonePe app. I told him that I didn't use any UP service but I do
know in's and out's about the app as my elder brother and parents used it. He asked me
if there is something missing in the app. He asked me for a start up, (they expect some
--- PAGE 4 ---
ideas that solve some real problems, also think of the business expect of it, on how it
would make its revenue and all). He asked me a few system design questions for the
most frequent app that I used on my phone. This interview focuses on your critical
thinking on different situations and interests towards the system design aspect as
PhonePe is a product based company.
Finally, 6 candidates received the job offer. All of our offers were i+p.

1. Stay calm and confident throughout the interview process. Focus on your

individual progress for the entire preparation phase and to not compare yourself
with others.

2. PhonePe interviews focus a lot on DSA. The only way to master it is to solve

more and more questions. There is no shortcut to it. Give more and more
contests. CP isn't a must, but it helps a lot.

3. Think out loud during the technical interviews. It's fine to ask for hints, when stuck

(hints are to get closer to the optimal approach, hints give ideas to go for which
approach, solve more questions to build that intuition).

4. Be well prepared for any format of the interviews, you can never expect only DP

or Graphs questions to be asked in the OA's, have a well understanding of other
topics as well. My round-3 was conducted right after my round-1 and before
round-2, so be prepared for all rounds beforehand, as some reordering might
happen.
All the best! Feel free to reach out!

--- PAGE 2 ---

3. Given a binary string of length 'n' and 'q' queries having ranges 1 to r. For every query, you

4. Given a directed graph and q queries of three types could i.e. Adding a dependency, removing

Approach:
i. I used an adjacency matrix for this as the queries involved addition and removal of
edges which can easily be done in O(1) time complexity.

complexity. The solution worked and all test cases were passed.
Overall I was able to solve 3 problems completely and 1 partially. 30 students were shortlisted
for the interviews after this round.

2. Technical Interview - 1(30 students appeared for this round)

The offline interviews were just on the next day after the OA. The interviews started at 9 am and
15 panels were going on simultaneously. The round started with me giving my introduction to
the panelist and then 2 DSA questions were asked.

1. Given n number of flowers having their blooming period as (start, end) inclusive. If a person

arrives in the garden at i time provide the number of flowers that the person would see.
Approach:
i. I started with the brute force approach of creating an array and incrementing the
number of flowers at a particular time by traversing through the provided flowers. But this
solution failed at some edge cases.
ii. The panelist provided me some hints to approach the solution through sorting the start
and end time of flowers. I finally used the prefix method to maintain the number of flowers at a
point of time.
ili. Further I was asked to provide the space and time complexity for the given solution.
The panelist was satisfied with my approach and we moved on to the next question.
--- PAGE 3 ---

2. Given a matrix of r rows and c cols we need to move from the (0, 0) to the (r-1, c-1) cell. We

can only make 2 moves, 1 towards right and 1 downwards. Each move is represented by an
alphabetH for horizontal and V for vertical move. The result of the program should be the kth
lexicographically smallest possible path out of all the paths.
Approach:
i. I started with the brute force approach where all the paths would be generated using the
dfs and then sorting the strings and returning the ith value.
ii. The panelist told me to improve this so after some discussion I tried to find a
mathematical way to reach the output but was not successful. So finally I decided to generate the
next permutations from the smallest possible path for i times.
ili. The panelist asked me to explain the implementation of the next _permutation function
and we discussed the same for 10 minutes.
Finally the panelist told me that time was up. The interview lasted for around 1 hr. Finally, 13
students were shortlisted for the next round.

Tips:

1. Always be vocal about the approach you are thinking about even if it is wrong.

2. Always make sure about all the conditions mentioned in the problem and ask doubts to the

panelist about the same.
